stimuli.text: Researchers want to investigate whether a new phone app reduces evening screen time. They have 60 volunteer students available.

Random samples of 15 were taken from two groups. The values of daily steps (thousands) are:

**Group 1:** 11, 12, 14, 15, 18, 22, 23, 27, 27, 27, 28, 28, 29, 29, 30

**Group 2:** 14, 16, 16, 17, 21, 21, 33, 34, 34, 36, 39, 39, 40, 44, 62
A school district claims that 40% of its students take public transit to school. A reporter suspects the true proportion is lower. In a random sample of 250 students, 93 take public transit.

Data were collected on outdoor temperature (°F) (x) and daily iced-drink sales (y) for a sample of days. A scatterplot shows a linear pattern, and the residual plot shows no pattern. Computer output for the least-squares regression is shown.

```text
Predictor   Coef      SE Coef
Constant    57.5
x           3.1
S = 5.1    R-Sq = 71.0%
```

questions.stem: A principal divides students by grade level and takes a simple random sample of 25 students from each grade. What sampling method is this?

options.why: Cluster sampling selects whole groups.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 230 teenagers in a state, 161 get at least 8 hours of sleep. Which is a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all teenagers in a state who get at least 8 hours of sleep?

options.why: Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 1.96.
Multiply the standard error by z*.
Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
Divide by n inside the square root.

questions.stem: In an experiment on a new reading program, students are first grouped by reading level, then randomly assigned to programs within each level. What is the purpose of grouping by level?

options.text: Blocking, to reduce variability caused by reading level
options.why: Correct. Blocking controls a known source of variation.
It remains an experiment.
Groups by level are not placebo groups.
That is a sampling idea.

questions.explanation: Blocking controls a known source of variation.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 300 customers of an online store, 198 would recommend it to a friend. Which is a 90% confidence interval for the proportion of all customers of an online store who would recommend it to a friend?

Divide by n inside the square root.

questions.stem: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.2 and P(A and B) = 0.1. What is P(A or B), and are A and B independent?

options.why: Subtract P(A and B) so the overlap is not counted twice.
Correct. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); independent if P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.1.
P(A and B) is not 0, so they are not mutually exclusive.
Compare P(A and B) with P(A)·P(B) = 0.1.

options.why: Correct. t has heavier tails to account for it.

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 174 of 280 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 62 of 240 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: Divide the difference by its standard error.
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).
The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.
Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.4538; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).

questions.stem: For a chi-square test of homogeneity on these counts, what are the test statistic and degrees of freedom?

Correct. χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E with df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1).

parts.prompt: Write an investigative question for this study, and identify the explanatory and response variables.

rubric.criterion: A clear investigative question that names the population or units and the variables.
rubric.example: "Does the app lead to a better average evening screen time over two weeks than no app for units like these?"
Explanatory: treatment (the app vs no app). Response: average evening screen time over two weeks.

parts.prompt: Explain why an experiment, rather than an observational study, should be used to answer the question.

rubric.criterion: Only random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion; an observational study could be confounded.
rubric.example: Units that choose a treatment may differ in other ways that affect the response.

parts.prompt: Describe how to randomly assign the 60 units to the two treatments in a completely randomized design.

rubric.example: Number units 1–60; use a random number generator to select 30 different numbers.
Those 30 receive the app; the remaining 30 receive no app.

parts.prompt: The researchers consider blocking by grade level (9th and 12th graders use phones differently). Explain how blocking would be carried out and why it could improve the experiment.

rubric.criterion: Form blocks and randomize within each block.
rubric.example: Separate units into the blocks, then randomly assign half of each block to each treatment.

rubric.criterion: Benefit: reduces variability in the response due to the blocking variable, making a treatment effect easier to detect.
rubric.example: Accounts for differences caused by grade level.

parts.prompt: Find the five-number summary for each group.
Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to determine whether Group 2 has any outliers. Show your work.

rubric.example: IQR = 22; upper fence = 39 + 1.5(22) = 72. No outliers.

parts.prompt: Compare the distributions of the two groups (shape, center and variability) in context.

rubric.example: The median for Group 2 (34) is greater than for Group 1 (27).
Group 2 is more variable (IQR 22 vs 13).

rubric.criterion: Comments on shape or unusual features.
rubric.example: Describes the shapes using the summaries.

parts.prompt: Which measure of center is more appropriate for Group 2, the mean or the median? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Median, because it is resistant to the outlier or skew.
rubric.example: Mean 31.1 is pulled toward the high value; median 34 is not.

parts.prompt: State the hypotheses, defining the parameter.

rubric.criterion: Correct hypotheses with the parameter defined.
rubric.example: H₀: p = 0.4; Hₐ: p < 0.4, where p is the proportion of all district students who take public transit.

parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate procedure and check its conditions.

rubric.criterion: One-sample z test for a proportion.
rubric.example: Random sample stated.
250 is less than 10% of all students (assumed); np₀ = 100 and n(1 − p₀) = 150 are both at least 10.

parts.prompt: Calculate the test statistic and p-value.
State a conclusion in context at α = 0.05.

rubric.criterion: Correct decision linked to the p-value, in context.
rubric.example: Because 0.1831 is greater than 0.05, fail to reject H₀: not convincing evidence that the proportion is less than 0.4.

parts.prompt: Write the equation of the least-squares regression line, defining the variables.

rubric.example: ŷ = 57.5 + 3.1x, where ŷ is predicted daily iced-drink sales and x is outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: Interpret the slope and the value of R-Sq in context.

rubric.example: For each additional unit of outdoor temperature (°F), the predicted daily iced-drink sales increases by about 3.1.
About 71.0% of the variation in daily iced-drink sales is accounted for by the linear model with outdoor temperature (°F).

parts.prompt: One observation has x = 10 and y = 91. Calculate and interpret its residual. Also find the correlation r.

rubric.example: ŷ = 88.5; residual = 91 − 88.5 = 2.5: the actual value is above the prediction.

parts.prompt: The data come from a convenience sample. Explain how this affects the conclusions and describe a better data collection method.

rubric.criterion: Results may not generalize to the population; a random sample would allow generalization.
rubric.example: Take a simple random sample of days from the population of interest. Observational data also cannot show causation.
